title: The Human Worker as Civilizational Nexus
author: Luke Burgis
summary: Luke Burgis argues that the debate about AI and work has focused too narrowly on job disruption and economic displacement, missing a deeper challenge: the disruption to the soul. Work has three dimensions—objective (what it produces), subjective (what it does to the worker), and transcendent (how it participates in something beyond the self)—and the AI era threatens to collapse all three if the human person is not at the center of the analysis. Lewis Mumford's insight that the clock, not the steam engine, began modernity, is invoked to argue that technologies are environments, not merely tools. Since Benedictine monastic time escaped the cloister and became money in the counting house, work has been progressively extracted from prayer and formation. AI now threatens to extract human agency from work itself. The proper measure of any technology is whether it helps the human person flourish—and families, not corporations, are the primary unit in which that flourishing is either supported or undermined.
points: The objective dimension of work (what it produces) has eclipsed the subjective dimension (what it does to the worker), and AI discourse accelerates that collapse by reducing 'work' to measurable output.
Machines can draft, summarize, reason, and report back, but nothing they do forms them—they are not becoming anything; this is the essential difference between human and machine work.
Technology is both a tool and an environment; the environment question—whether it is fit for the human person and builds rather than strips virtue—is the question AI discourse is avoiding.
The Benedictine principle Ora et labora (work and prayer) holds that work, properly sanctified, can become a form of prayer—a vision AI-age work urgently needs to recover.
The family is the first and most important site where the effects of technology on the human person are felt, yet it is the last place AI discourse looks.
quotes: But nothing it does is doing anything to it. It is not becoming anything.
Work has been and always will be a central part of what it means to be human, ever since we were given the command to cultivate the earth in the book of Genesis.
Work is also a deeply spiritual activity. Ora et labora, work and prayer, was central to the Benedictine tradition because work, properly understood, can become a form of prayer.
We must evaluate technologies by the subjective dimension too: how are they forming, or de-forming, the human person? Are they building virtues, or stripping them away?
The economy is for man, not man for the economy; likewise: technology is for humanity.
Work can be sanctified. Work done with excellence is a gift—not just to ourselves, but to others and even to God.
